title: TTL
subtitle: Time-To-Live expiration mechanics, active vs passive expiry in Redis, and TTL jitter to prevent cache avalanches.
keyTakeaways: Time-To-Live (TTL) acts as an automatic safety net that bounds data staleness and prevents dormant keys from permanently consuming cache memory.
Redis enforces TTLs using a hybrid of passive expiry (checking expiration upon key access) and active background sampling (purging expired keys periodically).
Setting identical TTLs across large key batches triggers a Cache Avalanche when they expire simultaneously; adding randomized jitter is mandatory.
architectureDiagram:
CACHE AVALANCHE MITIGATION VIA TTL JITTER
WITHOUT JITTER (Simultaneous Expiration -> DB Crash!):
Key 1 (TTL=3600s) ---+
Key 2 (TTL=3600s) ---+---> At T = 3600s: 100k keys vanish simultaneously!
Key 3 (TTL=3600s) ---+---> 100k requests hit Database at the exact same second (Crash)

WITH RANDOMIZED JITTER (Smooth Desynchronized Eviction):
Key 1 (TTL = 3600s + 42s)  -> Expires at 3642s
Key 2 (TTL = 3600s + 185s) -> Expires at 3785s  -> DB load distributed smoothly
Key 3 (TTL = 3600s + 291s) -> Expires at 3891s

sections.heading: How Caches Enforce Key Expiration Internally
sections.body: A common misconception is that a cache fires a timer interrupt the exact millisecond a key's TTL expires. Maintaining millions of concurrent hardware timers would overwhelm the CPU. Systems like Redis use a hybrid passive-active expiration strategy.
bullets: Passive Expiration: When a client issues a `GET key`, Redis checks its expiration timestamp in the dictionary. If expired, Redis immediately deletes the key from memory and returns nil to the caller.

Active Periodic Sampling: Ten times per second (by default in Redis), a background thread samples 20 random keys with an active TTL from the keyspace. Any expired keys found are evicted. If more than 25% of the sampled keys are expired, Redis immediately repeats the process to prevent memory exhaustion from unread keys.

sections.heading: Preventing Cache Avalanche and Memory Leaks
sections.body: Cache Avalanche occurs when thousands of cached entries expire at the exact same moment—typically because a batch worker pre-warmed millions of records at midnight with a static 24-hour TTL. When midnight strikes the following day, millions of keys vanish simultaneously, routing a catastrophic traffic spike directly to the backing database.
bullets: Randomized Jitter: Always add a random delta (e.g., ±10% or +0..300s) to baseline TTLs so expirations spread smoothly over time.
Memory Protection: Unbounded keys without TTLs eventually fill RAM, forcing the cache into eviction mode (`maxmemory-policy`), which can evict hot active keys.
Circuit Breakers: When a cache cluster fails or suffers an avalanche, protect backing databases using edge rate limiters and circuit breakers.

tradeOffs.pros: Minimal data staleness; near-instant convergence after database updates; prevents storing stale state.
tradeOffs.cons: Higher cache miss frequency; increased baseline read load on backing database.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Rapidly changing data like stock prices, seat availability, and online user presence.

tradeOffs.pros: Maximum cache hit ratio (99%+); shields databases from heavy read traffic; predictable p99 read performance.
tradeOffs.cons: Data remains stale until TTL expires unless explicit event-driven invalidation (CDC / pub-sub) is implemented.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Static product catalogs, postal code lookups, country lists, and CMS article bodies.

interviewTip: Whenever specifying a TTL during an architectural design, mention adding randomized jitter: 'We will set a baseline TTL of 1 hour with a randomized 5-minute jitter. This desynchronizes key expirations and prevents a cache avalanche from overwhelming our database.'
